coredata.dc:description: Bismuth oxyiodide/magnetite (BiOI/Fe3O4) nanocomposites were synthesized by a hydrothermal reaction. The synthesized BiOI/Fe3O4 was used to remove bisphenol A (BPA) from an aqueous solution under simulated solar light. The molar ratio of Bi to Fe in BiOI/Fe3O4 significantly affected BPA degradation, with the optimal BiOI/Fe3O4 (2:1) ratio in the composites. Optimum operating conditions such as a catalyst dosage of 1.0 g/L, an initial BPA concentration of 10 mg/L, and pH 7 gave a complete degradation of completely removed BPA within 30 min. The primary reactive oxygen species were verified as superoxide radicals and holes in oxidative species experiments. The magnetic BiOI/Fe3O4 could be easily collected from an aqueous solution by an external magnet, and its reusability was successfully demonstrated through recycling experiments. Furthermore, the derivatives in BiOI/Fe3O4 photocatalytic reactions were investigated, and a possible BPA degradation pathway was proposed. These results show that BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposites have great potential for BPA removal from water and wastewater treatment systems.

ce:section.ce:para: Bisphenol A (2,2-bis [4-hydroxyphenyl]propane, BPA) is a raw material of epoxy resin and polycarbonate for manufacturing consumer products and industrials (Michałowicz, 2014). Global BPA production is gradually increasing every year, with a high volume production of 7800 million tons in the plastic industry circa 2015 (Fang et al., 2020). BPA has frequently been detected in water and wastewater systems due to its wide-range industrial applications, causing toxic effects such as carcinogenesis, mutagenesis, heart diseases, immunotoxicity, and epigenetic modification on humans and organisms (Cuomo et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2019). Therefore, efficient treatment methods for removing BPA are necessary to prevent its adverse effects on water systems and human health. Several technologies, including adsorption (Kono et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2009; de Souza and Petri, 2018), reverse osmosis (Yüksel et al., 2013), microbial degradation (Ben Ali et al., 2021; Ferro Orozco et al., 2013), ozonation (Kusvuran and Yildirim, 2013), and photodegradation (Reddy et al., 2018), have been developed to remove BPA from water and wastewater systems. Among the available technologies, photocatalysis is considered as a promising method due to its effective degradation efficiency and mineralization of recalcitrant organic compounds. TiO2 has been widely used to degrade persistent organic pollutants in an aqueous solution (Fang et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2003). However, TiO2-based photocatalysts still have limitations regarding large band gap energy and inefficient charge separation, resulting in weak photocatalytic performance in the visible light region.

Bismuth oxyiodide (BiOI) is a prospective semiconductor, which uses visible light, unlike the traditional photocatalyst such as TiO2. BiOI compounds belong to a group of V–VI–VII ternary oxide semiconductors with layered crystal structures (Zhang et al., 2020b). In its particular layered crystal structure, (Bi2O2)2+ slabs are separated by double slabs of halogen atoms and the layered structure polarizes the related atoms and orbitals (Dai and Zhao, 2016). The intrinsic dipole of BiOI can lead to the formation of an internal static electric field and promote greater separation efficiency of the photoinduced electron–hole pairs, enhancing its photocatalytic activity (Luo et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2006). In general, the valence band of BiOI is composed of I 5p and O 2p orbitals, and its conduction band contains Bi 6p orbital. Therefore, the mass ratio (Bi:O:I) in bismuth oxyiodides determines the band structure and significantly influences its photocatalytic efficiency (Lee et al., 2015). Different kinds of bismuth oxyiodides, including BiOI, Bi4O5I2, Bi5O7I, and Bi7O9I3 have been synthesized. Among them, especially I-deficient bismuth oxyiodide has shown good photocatalytic activity regarding the degradation of organic pollutants (Cui et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2018). However, its practical application is still limited because of its intrinsic property of forming a colloid in water, making it difficult to separate the used photocatalysts from the mixture after sorption processes.

To overcome these limitations, magnetic BiOI composites were fabricated by anchoring BiOI to the surface of magnetite for BPA degradation and easy recovery of photocatalysts from a mixture. Fe3O4 nanoparticles have been used as a photocatalyst for different kinds of organic pollutants (Mishra et al., 2016; Moztahida et al., 2019a,b). Magnetite nanoparticles can serve as photocatalytic materials under visible light because of their small band gap energy (Mirzaei et al., 2017). By doping the metal oxide catalyst with another catalytic substances, the typical recombination of electron–hole pairs in bare Fe3O4 can be reduced, improving photocatalytic performance (Mishra and Chun, 2015; Yao et al., 2014). In addition, magnetic Fe3O4 particles can be easily recovered by an external magnet.

In this work, magnetically separable BiOI composites were synthesized via a hydrothermal method and were used to degrade BPA from an aqueous solution under simulated solar light. The synthesized BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposites were characterized by several instrumental techniques. The effects of different operating parameters such as BiOI/Fe3O4 dose, pH, and initial BPA concentration during photocatalytic processes under simulated solar light were investigated. The oxidation intermediates of BPA degradation were also observed to identify a possible BPA degradation pathway.

Bisphenol A (BPA, ≥99%) and potassium iodide (KI, 99%) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich, USA. Bismuth nitrate pentahydrate (Bi(NO3)3·5H2O, ≥98%) was purchased from Junsei Chemical Co., Ltd, Japan. Iron (Ⅱ) chloride tetrahydrate (FeCl2·4H2O, 99%), iron (Ⅲ) chloride hexahydrate (FeCl3·6H2O, 98%), and ethylene glycol (C2H6O2, 99%) were purchased from Daejung Chemicals & Materials Co., Ltd, South Korea. Ammonia water (NH4OH, 30%) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH, ≥93%) were purchased from Duksan Pure Chemicals Co., Ltd, South Korea.

Magnetic nanoparticles (Fe3O4) were prepared using a simple chemical coprecipitation method. In 200-mL nitrogen-purged water, 10 mmol of FeCl3·6H2O and 5 mmol of FeCl2·4H2O were dissolved. After complete dissolution, 5 mL of NH4OH was injected into the mixture under sonication, and the color was rapidly changed from yellow to black. The formed precipitate was washed until the solution pH reached 7, separated by an external magnetic field, and dried at 60 °C for 24 h. BiOI/Fe3O4 composites were synthesized using a hydrothermal method. In 25 mL of ethylene glycol, 2 mmol of Bi(NO3)3·5H2O was added, and the as-prepared Fe3O4 nanoparticles in a different molar ratio of Bi to Fe (1:2, 1:1, and 2:1) was dispersed in the suspension and stirred for sufficient contact between Bi3+ and Fe3O4. Then, 10 mL of ethylene glycol containing 2 mmol of KI was dropwisely added to the suspension and the pH value was adjusted to 7 using 1 M NaOH as our preliminary experiments gave the highest photocatalytic activity at pH 7 (Fig. S1). Finally, the mixture was transferred to a 100 mL Teflon-lined stainless autoclave and heated in an oven at 150 °C for 6 h. After the reaction was completed and the autoclave had cooled, the products were separated by filtration, washed with distilled water and ethanol several times to remove ionic species, and then dried at 60 °C in the oven. BiOI was prepared using the same procedure without adding Fe3O4 nanoparticles. The overall BiOi/Fe3O4 synthetic procedure was descibed in Fig. S2.

The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the photocatalysts were determined using an X-ray diffractometer (D/Max-2500, Rigaku, Japan) from 5° to 80° with a Cu Ka radiation (λ = 1.5406). The elements on the surface were explored by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, NEXSA, ThermoFisher, USA). The chemical bonding in the synthesized composites was investigated via Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR, Frontier, PerkinElmer, USA). Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, SU8220, Hitachi, Japan) was used to obtain the morphologies of the materials. The specific surface area and pore size distribution were determined using the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) analysis and Barrett-Joyner-Halenda method with nitrogen adsorption/desorption isotherms (BELSORP-max, MicrotracBEL, Japan). The zeta potential of the photocatalysts was evaluated using a zeta potential and particle size analyzer (Otsuka Electronics Co. Ltd., ELSZ-2000ZS, Japan). The photoluminescence (PL) was measured by spectrofuluorophotometry (RF-6000, Shimadzu, Japan) and UV–vis diffuse reflection spectra (UV–vis DRS) were obtained at room temperature using a UV–vis spectrophotometer (UV-2600, Shimadzu, Japan) with BaSO4 as reference. A magnetic property measurement system (MSPS, 7404, Lake Shore, USA) was used at room temperature with an applied field between −15,000 and 15,000 Oe.

The photocatalytic activity of BiOI/Fe3O4 was investigated by photocatalytic degradation of BPA under simulated solar light. The 150-W xenon arc lamp (UXL-150MO, USHIO, USA) was used as a light source, and irradiation was provided by a solar simulator (10500, ABET technologies, USA). Photodegradation experiments were conducted with 1.0 g/L of the catalyst and 10-mg/L BPA solution. The suspension was stirred in the dark for 30 min before irradiation to ensure adsorption–desorption equilibrium. The samples were withdrawn and filtered with a 0.22-μm PVDF disposable filter. The effects of operating parameters such as BiOI/Fe3O4 dosage, initial BPA concentration, and pH on BPA degradation were investigated. The pH was adjusted to 3–9 using 0.1-M HCl and 0.1-M NaOH. Photodegradation experiments were performed in triplicate and the average values were used to calculate the photodegradation rate. The residue BPA concentration was analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, DGU-20A3, Shimadzu, Japan) equipped with a C18 column (Agilent Eclipse XDB-C18 4.6 × 150 mm, 5 μm) and UV detector (absorbance wavelength: 277 nm). The column was maintained at 35 °C during analysis. The isocratic acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid in water (70:30) at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min were used as the mobile phase. The total organic carbon of the degraded solution was determined by TOC analyzer (wario TOC cube, Elementar, Germany).

The radical trapping experiment was performed to identify active species generated in the photocatalytic system by adding different types of chemical scavengers. Benzoquinone (BQ), ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), methanol (MeOH), and sodium azide (SA) were used as scavengers for superoxide radical (•O2 −), holes (h+), hydroxyl radical (•OH), and singlet oxygen (1O2), respectively. The concentration of all scavenger solutions was 1 mmol/L.

To explore the photodegradation mechanism of BPA, the intermediates generated in the photocatalytic reaction were analyzed using a liquid chromatography–mass spectrometer (LC-MS, XEVO-TQS micro, Waters, USA) in a negative electrospray ionization mode with a scan range of m/z 50–300. The BEH C18 column (3.0 × 50 mm, 1.7 μm) was used, and the temperature of the column was maintained at 40 °C. The mobile phase was a mixture of 0.1% NH4OH in water (A) and 0.1% NH4OH in methanol (B) following a gradient: 0–3 min: 50% A; 3–5.1 min: 5% A; 5.1–7 min: 50% at 0.5 mL/min of the flow rate. The ionization source temperature was 150 °C and cone voltage was 20 V.

XRD analysis was performed to identify the crystal structure of Fe3O4, BiOI, and BiOI/Fe3O4 (Fig. S3(a)). The XRD pattern of Fe3O4 showed diffraction peaks at 2 theta of 18.4° 30.2°, 35.6°, 43.3°, 53.8°, 57.3°, 62.9°, 71.4°, and 74.4° corresponding cubic magnetite (Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD) 75–0449). In the case of BiOI and BiOI/Fe3O4, the characteristic peaks at 2 theta of 9.33°, 23.93°, 28.86°, 31.55°, 37.08°, 45.06°, 49.47°, 54.50°, 59.98°, 65.83°, 73.46°, and 74.81° matched with ICSD 73–2062 for tetragonal bismuth oxyiodide. The strong peaks at 28.86° and 31.55° were shifted slightly to lower diffraction angles than those of ICSD 73–2062 (Fig. S3(a)); pH adjustment caused the substitution of I− with OH− and consequently caused expansion and structure distortion (Wu et al., 2018). The BiOI/Fe3O4 pattern showed a weak characteristic Fe3O4 peak at 35.6°, indicating the presence of Fe3O4 in the composites. Moreover, FE-SEM analysis indicated that both BiOI and BiOI/Fe3O4 were composed of irregular plates and rods (Fig. S4).

The surface chemical structure of BiOI/Fe3O4(2:1) were revealed by XPS characterization (Fig. S5). The total survey spectrum of BiOI/Fe3O4(2:1) showed the presence of Bi, O, I, C, and Fe (Fig. S5(a)). The Bi 4f spectrum had major two peaks at 158.8 and 164.1 eV, which were assigned to Bi 4f7/2 and 4f5/2, respectively (Fig. S5(b)), implying that the Bi atoms in BiOI/Fe3O4 is Bi3+ (Chang et al., 2013). The O 1s spectrum showed three peaks at 529.3, 529.8, and 530.9 eV, which were assigned to Bi–O, Fe–O, and lattice oxygen, respectively (Fig. S5(c)) (Gao et al., 2017c; Luo et al., 2017). The spectra of the I 3d region displayed two peaks at binding energies of 618.8 eV and 630.3 eV, corresponding to the I 3d5/2 and I 3d3/2, respectively (Fig. S5(d)) (Chang et al., 2013; Lan et al., 2020). The peak at 710.9 eV was assigned to Fe 2p3/2 (Fig. S5(e)) (Gao et al., 2017a).

Fig. S3(b) shows FT-IR spectra of BiOI, BiOI/Fe3O4, and Fe3O4. The wide peak at 3386 cm−1 was assigned to the vibration of hydroxyl groups (O–H) or absorbed water. The peaks at approximately 3000 cm−1 and 1500 cm−1 were C–H and C–OH bonds, respectively, which originated from ethylene glycol residue (Mishra et al., 2016). The adsorption bands at 884 cm−1, 1068 cm−1, and 1322 cm−1 represent the stretching bonds of Bi–O, indicating Bi–O–Bi, Bi–O–I, and Bi–O–Fe in BiOI and BiOI/Fe3O4 (Mirzaei et al., 2017; Moztahida et al., 2019b). The stretching vibration of Fe–O bonds in BiOI/Fe3O4 and Fe3O4 was attributed to the intense band at 546 cm−1, confirming that Fe3O4 and BiOI were successfully combined to form the BiOI/Fe3O4 composite (Moztahida et al., 2019b). The broad band between 2000 cm−1 and 2300 cm−1 observed on all samples might be generated from CO2 in the atmosphere (Mishra and Chun, 2015).

As shown in Fig. 1 (a), the absorbance spectra of BiOI decreased rapidly at approximately 500 nm, whereas BiOI/Fe3O4 was excited throughout the visible light range. The adsorption ability was significantly improved in the case of BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposites compared with bare Fe3O4 nanoparticles. However, the amount of BPA adsorbed in BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposites was almost similar. The successful photodegradation of BPA by the BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposite may be attributed to the rapid adsorption of the former on the nanocomposites' surface via π–π conjugation followed by diffusion to the surface of the photocatalysts (Ziegmann and Frimmel, 2010).

Without the photocatalysts, BPA degradation efficiency was only 1% after 2 h irradiation, indicating that BPA was not prone to direct photolysis. Both Fe3O4 nanoparticles and BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposites gave similar adsorption capacity for BPA removal. The photodegradation capacity of magnetite nanoparticles alone was nearly negligible under solar light. The synthesized BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposites dramatically improved the photocatalytic degradation of BPA, achieving almost complete BPA removal from the solution within 1 h. Especially, the Bi to Fe molar ratio in the photocatalysts substantially affected BPA photocatalytic degradation, and BiOI/Fe3O4 (2:1) provided nearly complete BPA degradation within 30 min. The rate of photodegradation of BiOI/Fe3O4 (2:1) (k app = 0.0795 min−1) was significantly higher than that of both BiOI/Fe3O4 (1:1) and BiOI/Fe3O4 (1:2) (k app = 0.0335 and 0.0299 min−1, respectively) (Table 1). Therefore, BiOI/Fe3O4 (2:1) with a higher rate and efficiency of degradation was selected for further experiments.

The effect of catalyst dose on BPA degradation was investigated at a constant initial BPA concentration (10 mg/L) and pH 7 (Fig. 3 (a)). BPA photodegradation was improved as the amount of photocatalyst was increased from 0.1 to 1.0 g/L. However, as the amount of BiOI/Fe3O4 nanoparticles was beyond 1.0 g/L, a decrease in the photodegradation rate was observed. This decrease in the degradation rate can be attributed to an increase in the turbidity of the solution, which retards light penetration and hence decreases efficiency (Moztahida et al., 2019a,b; Nawaz et al., 2020). This indicates that an optimum amount of BiOI/Fe3O4 nanoparticles must be used to obtain maximum photodegradation of the pollutant.

The initial concentration of the pollutant has a significant effect on the rate of photocatalytic degradation. The effect of the concentration of BPA on the rate of degradation was investigated by varying BPA concentrations (10, 20, and 30 mg/L) and maintaining the amount of BiOI/Fe3O4 composite (1.0 g/L) at pH 7. The adsorption of BPA on BiOI/Fe3O4 was slightly improved, but the rate of photodegradation was significantly decreased with an increase in the concentration of BPA, as shown in Fig. 3(b). With the initial BPA concentration of 10 mg/L, complete BPA degradation was achieved within 30 min. However, a lower rate of BPA degradation was observed with higher concentrations of BPA due to the decreased availability of reactive radicals (Jang et al., 2020).

To evaluate the effect of initial pH values, the photocatalytic degradation experiment was conducted with a pH range from 3 to 9, and BiOI/Fe3O4 showed high efficiencies of removal over the entire considered pH range (Fig. 3(c)). As the pH value increases from 3 to 7, a nearly complete removal of BPA was achieved, and a significant increase in the rate of photodegradation rate (k
app ) from 0.0256 to 0.115 min−1 was observed (Table S1). As oxygen could readily accept electrons from the synthesized nanocomposites to produce reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as •O2 −, hydrogen peroxide, and •OH, these ROS played an important role in transforming the contaminants (Jang et al., 2020). The increasing pH favors the generation of •O2 −, increasing the efficiency of BPA degradation. However, as the pH was further increased from 7 to 9, a negative effect of alkaline pH on the rate of photodegradation (k
app = 0.0917 min−1) was observed. Moreover, some studies have reported that the rate of photodegradation under different initial pH values was related to the zeta potential of the catalyst surface and charge of ionic BPA (Wang and Lim, 2010). As the dissociation constant pKa1 and pKa2 of BPA are 9.6 and 11.2, respectively, BPA typically prevails as an anion at acidic and neutral pH (Lv et al., 2019). The point of zero charge (PZC) of BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposite occurred at pH 8.3 (Fig. S8). The overall surface charge on BiOI/Fe3O4 was negative when the pH was greater than the PZC of the nanocomposite. Therefore, repulsive forces due to the similar charges of pollutant and the composite material might decrease the rate of photodegradation. The efficiency of photodegradation of BPA by BiOI/Fe3O4 nanoparticles in this study was compared with those obtained in previous studies (Table 2 ). The efficiency of photodegradation of the nanocomposites under solar light was higher than that of most of the catalysts reported previously. In addition, the TOC removal was 19% at neutral pH.

To investigate the stability and reusability of BiOI/Fe3O4 composites, the nanocomposites were reused four times under solar light irradiation. The BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposite was easily separated from the BPA solution using an external magnet. The photocatalytic activities of the nanocomposite remained unchanged in the second cycle, but a 7.8% decrease from its initial performance was observed in the fourth cycle (Fig. S9(a)). Furthermore, the stability of the BiOI/Fe3O4 composite was evaluated by comparing XRD patterns before and after the recycling experiment. As presented in Fig. S9(b), there was no obvious change in the two XRD patterns, indicating that the structure of magnetic BiOI/Fe3O4 remains intact and stable. This confirms that the synthesized magnetic BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposite, which can be easily separated from the solution, could give a practical applications in water remediation.

To explore the role of ROS in BPA photodegradation, a series of reactive radical trapping experiments was conducted by adding different scavengers (Jang et al., 2020; Lv et al., 2019). SA, MeOH, BQ, and EDTA were added to the reaction mixture to quench 1O2, •OH, •O2 −, and h+, respectively. A series of experiments revealed that the chemical scavengers inhibited the photodegradation of BPA in order of •O2 − radicals > h+ > 1O2 > •OH radicals (Fig. 4 ). The role of •O2 − radical and h+ was dominant in removing BPA. After the addition of BQ and EDTA, BPA removal was significantly inhibited, achieving only 19.9% and 29.6% removal efficiency, respectively, compared with when no scavenger was used. With the addition of MeOH, the efficiency reduction was only 9.3%, indicating that •OH radicals were the least dominant species during the degradation of BPA using the BiOI/Fe3O4 composite. These results suggest that all four ROS (•O2 −, h+, 1O2, and •OH) were produced, which could be ascribed to the efficient charge separation during the photocatalytic process and contribute to the degradation process. The stepwise photocatalytic mechanism for BiOI/Fe3O4 nanocomposites was proposed as follows:
(5) BiOI/Fe3O4 + hν → BiOI/Fe3O4 (e− CB + h + VB)
(6) BiOI/Fe3O4 + hν → BiOI/Fe3O4 (e− CB) + O2 → •O2 −
(7)
•O2 − + 2H+ → O2 + H2O2
(8) e− CB + H2O2→ •OH + OH−
(9) H2O + h + VB → •OH + H+
(10)
•O2 − + h + VB → 1O2
(11)
•O2 − + BPA → Degraded products
(12) h + VB + BPA → Degraded products

The overall degradation process depended on the charge separation across the interface of BiOI/Fe3O4 heterojunction (Gao et al., 2017b). Particularly, the photogenerated holes and •O2 − radicals participated in BPA degradation. The incorporation of magnetite into BiOI composites showed a synergistic effect of charge separation and increased photocatalytic capacity, which caused high BPA degradation efficiency.

BPA degradation intermediates were identified using the mass spectra obtained from the LC-MS-MS analyses (Figs. S10 and S11). Based on the identified degradation products, a BPA degradation scheme is presented in Fig. 5 , and detailed information about the intermediates is summarized in Table S2. As the principal active species were •O2 − radicals and holes, the degradation process began with the addition of either •O2 − radicals or holes to the BPA parent molecule (m/z: 227), and the degradation of BPA could be divided into two possible routes, forming 4-(2-Methyl-3-methylidenepent-4-en-2-yl)phenol (m/z: 189) and 2-methoxybenzene-1,4-diol (m/z: 141).

During BPA photodegradation by BiOI/Fe3O4, the ROS (•O2 −, h+, 1O2, and •OH radicals) were generated, and these radicals were involved in the reaction. The degradation of BPA can be divided into two possible routes. In route Ⅰ, the radicals oxidized the phenolic ring of BPA and formed intermediate B (4-(2-Methyl-3-methylidenepent-4-en-2-yl)phenol, m/z: 189). Through further C–C bond cleavage and hydroxylation, intermediate B was degraded into intermediate C (4-prop-1-en-2-ylphenol, m/z: 133) and intermediate D (4-(2-hydroxypropan-2-yl)phenol, m/z: 151) were generated (Zhang et al., 2020a). •O2 − radicals oxidized intermediate D to form intermediate F (4-(prop-1-en-2-yl)cyclohexa-3,5-diene-1,2-dione, m/z: 147) (Tijani et al., 2017). Moreover, intermediates D and E underwent hydroxylation to generate intermediate G (Benzene-1,4-diol, m/z: 109) (Zhang et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2018). In route Ⅱ, BPA was attacked by the radicals, forming intermediate C (2-methoxybenzene-1,4-diol, m/z: 141). Through oxidation, intermediate C was decomposed into intermediate F (4-(prop-1-en-2-yl)cyclohexa-3,5-diene-1,2-dione, m/z: 147). Subsequently, the phenyl rings of generated intermediates G and F were opened and decomposed into products H (Heptanoic acid, m/z: 127), I (Butan-2-ol, m/z: 75, J (Ethane-1,2-diol, m/z: 62), and K (Acetic acid, m/z: 127) (Diao et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020b; Zhang et al., 2018). These small molecular fractions were identified as the end products of the photodegradation process, which could be subsequently converted into fully oxidized products, i.e., carbon dioxide and water.

In this study, BiOI/Fe3O4 composites were successfully synthesized via a simple hydrothermal method. The molar ratio of Bi to Fe in BiOI/Fe3O4 significantly impacted BPA photodegradation, and BiOI/Fe3O4 (2:1) completely removed BPA within 30 min under simulated solar light at catalyst dosage (1.0 g/L), initial BPA concentration (10 mg/L), and pH 7. The major reactive species responsible for BPA degradation were also identified by adding radical scavengers to the experiments; •O2 − radicals and holes were identified as the primary reactive species. Magnetic BiOI/Fe3O4 composites were easily separated from an aqueous solution using an external magnet after BPA photodegradation. The high stability and easy recyclability of the nanocomposites enabled their reusability without any significant decrease in photodegradation capacity. The proposed degradation mechanism explained the degradation pathways as well as the formation of possible intermediates. The successful synthesis of magnetic BiOI/Fe3O4 composites and the corresponding high photodegradation of recalcitrant BPA open up new avenues for promoting their use to address other environmental issues.
